title: Future-task auxiliary reward with an inaction baseline
description: Give the agent an auxiliary reward for how well it could still achieve possible future tasks (here: reaching each state) when the episode ends, compared with what an agent that did nothing would be able to achieve. Destroying options, like breaking a vase or pushing a box into a corner, lowers that reward. The inaction baseline removes the incentive to stop other changes from happening. Prediction: fewer irreversible side effects than an observed-reward maximizer, like relative reachability; like it, no help against the reversible absent-supervisor shortcut.

source.title: Avoiding Side Effects By Considering Future Tasks
